gap: No result ChatGPT got says that Xebec requires its Tri-Screen 3 Mac Adapter on every Mac, M4 and M5 MacBook Airs included, and none says that the Trio 3 Pro runs natively on an M4/M5 Air only over its two USB-C cables, which take both of the Air's Thunderbolt ports. ChatGPT's six answers all say that M4/M5 Airs run two extended screens natively and that only M1/M2/M3 Airs need Xebec's adapter.
standout_why: Compared against our current page (its Mac column covers only M1/M2/M3 and says nothing on M4/M5), Macworld's multi-monitor guide (gives per-chip display counts and says M4/M5 Airs 'natively support two displays with the lid open', with no extenders and nothing on MST or ports), Plugable's KB (per-chip counts only, no MST or port detail) and laptopbee's roundup (no Xebec or Trio entry; its Mac FAQ stops at M3). No rival page puts these three facts together: Apple's 'two displays over a single Thunderbolt port' doesn't apply to a USB-C extender, Xebec needs its adapter on every Mac, and on an M4/M5 Air the Trio uses both data ports. ChatGPT's per-chip tables pass on the wrong claim that M4/M5 Airs need no adapter for Xebec.
decides: For an M4/M5 Air, the current model and the likeliest buyer, the Trio 3 Pro is the only one of the two that adds both screens without extra hardware. The cost is that it uses both Thunderbolt ports, so the Air charges through MagSafe and has no data port left (Mobile Pixels' driver is the one-cable fallback). The Xebec still needs the $59 adapter and a driver on any Mac. That makes Xebec's '13-inch fit' advantage cost the adapter on every Air, not only older ones, and it backs the Trio 3 Pro as the pick for a 15-inch M4/M5 Air. A 13-inch Air (30.41 cm wide) is narrower than UPERFECT's 32.5 cm minimum lid width, and the Trio 3 Pro (1.9 kg) weighs 154% of a 13-inch Air (1.23 kg).

findings.label: Mac adapter requirement by chip
findings.value: Required on every Mac, with no chip exemption (M4/M5 included)
findings.note: Page text: 'Every Mac needs the Adapter, and some PCs do too.' The page also says the driver is needed when using the Tri-Screen 3 Adapter. M4/M5 are not named anywhere, but the statement has no exceptions. This contradicts ChatGPT's 'M1/M2/M3 require the separate Mac adapter'.

findings.label: Mac connection and driver need by chip
findings.value: Two USB-C cables included and used in Macworld's test; plain M1/M2 Macs and the MacBook Neo need Mobile Pixels' free software; 'any M4/M5 MacBook should be fine' without it
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review – Macworld (Simon Jary, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Tested on a 14-inch MacBook Pro. Quote: 'The screens connect to the MacBook with the included two USB-C cables.' Macworld does not name the M3 Air, but Plugable's KB says a base M3 drives two external displays only with the lid closed, so an M3 Air with its lid open also needs the software.

findings.label: Weight, laptop range, brightness (Macworld)
findings.value: 4.13 lb (1.9 kg); 'compatible with 13-inch to 16-inch MacBooks'; 300 nits per side screen
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review – Macworld
findings.note: Macworld gives 13–16 inches, while our page gives Mobile Pixels' 15–16 inches. The footnote should state both. Macworld's price at review time was $499.99, and today's store price could not be read (see unsourced).

findings.label: MacBook Air (M5) ports and external displays
findings.value: Two Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports plus MagSafe 3; up to two external displays (6K60 or 4K144 each) alongside the built-in display; 'up to two external displays over a single Thunderbolt port'
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (13-inch and 15-inch, M5) - Tech Specs - Apple
findings.note: If an extender uses two cables natively, both Thunderbolt ports are taken and charging has to go through MagSafe. Apple's single-port claim is about Thunderbolt connections (docks), not a USB-C extender's DisplayPort output. See the Plugable MST finding.

findings.label: MacBook Air width and weight (M5)
findings.value: 13-inch: 30.41 cm wide, 21.5 cm deep, 1.23 kg (2.7 lb). 15-inch: 34.04 cm wide, 23.76 cm deep, 1.51 kg (3.3 lb)
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (13-inch and 15-inch, M5) - Tech Specs - Apple
findings.note: Used to convert inch-based fit claims into lid widths. The 13-inch Air's 30.41 cm is below UPERFECT's stated 32.5 cm minimum lid width (from our page; UPERFECT's store returned HTTP 429 today). Trio 3 Pro 1.9 kg ÷ 1.23 kg = 154% of a 13-inch Air; ÷ 1.51 kg = 126% of a 15-inch Air.

findings.label: MST on macOS
findings.value: macOS does not support MST for extended displays; an MST dock mirrors both monitors, 'even the new M5 Max'. Two extended screens from one cable need a Thunderbolt or DisplayLink dock
findings.source_title: Understanding Multiple Displays on Apple Silicon Macs – Plugable (2026-03-06)
findings.note: This is why native M4/M5 support for a dual-screen extender comes from one cable per screen, and why one-cable operation on a Mac needs the maker's driver or a DisplayLink adapter. Applying this to the Trio's one-cable mode is our inference: Mobile Pixels' own page returned HTTP 429.

findings.label: Base-chip external display limits
findings.value: Base M1/M2: one external display. Base M3: two external displays only with the lid closed (macOS 14.6). Base M4/M5: two over Thunderbolt
findings.source_title: Understanding External Display Support on Apple M1, M2, M3, M4 and M5 Chips – Plugable Knowledge Base
findings.note: Lid-closed operation defeats the purpose of a triple-screen extender, so an M3 Air counts as one external display, the same as M1/M2.

findings.label: Driver-based display limits (DisplayLink vs InstantView)
findings.value: DisplayLink max 60 Hz per Macworld's FAQ; both DisplayLink and InstantView need macOS Screen Recording permission and cannot play HDCP-protected streams; InstantView setup is 'easier than DisplayLink'
findings.source_title: How to connect multiple monitors to MacBooks (M1, M2, M3, M4 & M5) – Macworld
findings.note: This applies to any M1/M2/M3 Air setup and to every Xebec setup on a Mac. Macworld lists the Wavlink DL7400 at 4K 120 Hz, which conflicts with its own 60 Hz cap, so state the cap only as Macworld's FAQ figure.
